fabric_blog:225ab7984001.title: Announcing support for Materialized views and streaming tables in Mirrored Azure Databricks catalog
fabric_blog:225ab7984001.excerpt:
Access more Unity Catalog objects through the existing mirrored catalog experience in Microsoft Fabric

We are expanding Mirrored Azure Databricks catalogs in Microsoft Fabric to support materialized views and streaming tables alongside tables.

These objects remain created and managed in Azure Databricks, while Fabric provides read-only access to the underlying data through shortcuts. This brings more of your Unity Catalog environment into Fabric without copying or replicating the data.

What's new

A Mirrored Azure Databricks catalog can now include support:

  • Tables
  • Materialized views
  • Streaming tables

When configuring the mirrored catalog, select the Unity Catalog catalogs, schemas, and supported objects you want to make available in Fabric. Fabric mirrors the selected catalog structure and creates shortcuts to the underlying data.

This enhancement uses the existing Mirrored Azure Databricks catalog item and configuration workflow. There is no separate Fabric item type for materialized views or streaming tables.

Why this matters

Materialized views store precomputed results that can simplify recurring analytical queries. Streaming tables continuously process incoming data and maintain updated results for scenarios that require fresher information. Both object types can play an important role in the datasets that organizations publish for analytics and reporting.

Supporting these objects in a mirrored catalog gives Fabric users access to more of the curated data already available in Azure Databricks. It also allows platform teams to preserve clear ownership: Azure Databricks remains responsible for creating and processing the source objects, while Fabric provides experiences for discovering and analyzing the available data.

Prepare objects for external access

Before a materialized view or streaming table can appear in Fabric, configure it for external data access in Azure Databricks, complete the applicable prerequisites, and grant the required Unity Catalog permissions to the identity used by Fabric. Then refresh or synchronize the mirrored catalog.

Work with data in Fabric

The mirrored catalog includes an automatically generated SQL analytics endpoint for exploring and querying the available data with T-SQL. You can also create a Power BI semantic model and use Direct Lake mode for reporting.

Keep catalog changes in sync

For new mirrors, automatic synchronization of future catalog changes for the selected schema is enabled by default. Supported additions and deletions of schemas, tables, materialized views, and streaming tables can be reflected in Fabric when they meet the configured selection and external-access requirements.

Get started

Follow Tutorial: Configure Microsoft Fabric mirror from Azure Databricks Unity Catalog to create or configure your mirrored catalog. Review Microsoft Fabric Mirrored Catalog from Azure Databricks for prerequisites and external-access guidance.

fabric_blog:6a85cab2008a.title: Adding the Context Streaming Events Need: Reference Data Joins with OneLake Delta Tables in Fabric Eventstream
fabric_blog:6a85cab2008a.excerpt:
Enrich events with business context in real time, enabling faster decisions, more relevant alerts, and lower operational effort downstream. 

A real-time event tells you what happened. Context tells you what it means—and what to do next. In cold-chain logistics, a temperature reading becomes actionable when paired with a shipment’s temperature limits, customer priority, and response contacts. Reference Data Join in Fabric Eventstream brings that context to live events by matching them with business information from Delta tables in OneLake before they reach downstream destinations—so consumers can understand and act on the events without performing separate lookups.

The scenario: Cold chain logistics 

Cold chain logistics moves temperature-sensitive goods, such as fresh produce, dairy, frozen foods, and pharmaceuticals, from origin to destination within strict temperature ranges. Refrigerated trailers, containers, and warehouses must keep products in range at every stage. A few degrees off for too long can spoil a shipment, break compliance requirements, or put patient safety at risk. 

Refrigerated fleet continuously stream sensor telemetry. But a reading alone does not identify the shipment, its temperature limits, or the team responsible for responding. 

An alert without the context

An alert arrives from a refrigerated trailer: "Device TRL-4471 reported 9.2°C." Is the cargo at risk? Which customer is affected? Who should respond? The reading alone can't tell you. 

Figure: A raw temperature alert does not provide enough business context for immediate action.

The missing context --assets, shipments, routes, customers, and response contact already lives in Delta tables in OneLake. Reference Data Join brings that information into Fabric Eventstream before events reach downstream consumers.  

In this illustrative scenario, the trailer carries fresh produce with a configured transport range of 2–8°C for this shipment. A 9.2°C reading is therefore an excursion that operators can assess using the shipment details and assigned response team. 

The pattern is simple: combine live events with business context, then let downstream rules and workflows decide who needs to act.

For example, “TRL-4471: 9.2°C” becomes “Trailer TR-0918: 9.2°C; fresh produce; transport range 2–8°C; Northwind Foods; Tier 1; assigned response contacts.” A downstream rule can compare the reading with the shipment’s limits, flag the excursion, and notify the relevant team. 

The common workaround and tradeoffs 

Reference data can be joined either while events are in motion or after they land in a store. The right choice depends on when the business needs context. 

Land events first, then join for analytics. This approach keeps event payloads lean and avoids duplicating reference attributes on every record. It works well when analysis can wait until the data reaches downstream where it will be enriched. However, it adds a processing step and delays context that stream-based alerts, routing, and automated actions need immediately. 

Enrich events in the stream for time-sensitive scenarios. When alerts, routing, or automated actions must happen in real time, enriching events in motion provides the business context needed to respond immediately. It also creates complete, denormalized events that downstream consumers can use without repeating the join. The trade-off is larger payloads and duplicated reference values, which can increase transport and storage costs and require careful handling as reference data changes. 

For cold-chain monitoring, stream analytics is critical because a temperature excursion can require action before the event reaches storage. Enriching telemetry in Eventstream gives downstream detection and response workflows the cargo limits, customer priority, route, and contact context needed to assess the event immediately. If the use case is historical reporting rather than time-sensitive intervention, joining after ingestion may be the better design. 

 Introducing Reference Data Join In Fabric Eventstream

Reference Data Join lets you join a live stream with reference data stored as Delta tables in OneLake. The reference data appears as its own node on the Eventstream canvas. You join it to your stream inside the pipeline, before the data reaches any destination. 

  • Use OneLake Delta tables. Reuse master data exposed through a Lakehouse, including native tables and shortcuts to data in other workspaces, without copying the data. 
  • Choose no-code or SQL joins. Map keys visually for simple lookups or write SQL for advanced logic. 
  • Select inner or left outer joins. Keep the matching events for downstream processing or preserve every event and flag missing reference data. 
  • Add multiple reference data nodes. Add all the required context to the stream by adding one or more reference data nodes to the topology.  
  • Preview and validate on the canvas. Inspect reference rows and joined output before publishing. 
  • Control columns and refresh intervals. Load only the columns you need and keep slowly changing reference data current by configuring the refresh interval. 

Building the pipeline in few simple steps

Using the cold-chain logistics scenario, we’ll build a real-time pipeline that enriches raw trailer telemetry with Reference Data Join. In this example, an eventstream receives live TrailerTelemetry events from Azure IoT Hub, joined with reference data in Onelake, and sends the enriched records downstream. The following steps show the core pattern; the linked Microsoft Learn guide provides the full setup instructions. 

  1. Add the reference data node. In Edit mode, select Add source and choose Reference Data. A new node appears on the canvas next to your live stream.
Figure: Add a Reference Data source to the Eventstream canvas.
  1. Point it to a Delta table in OneLake. Select the Lakehouse that exposes the reference data, then choose the Delta table you want to use. 

The table can be: 

  • Natively stored in the selected Lakehouse. 
  • A shortcut to a Delta table stored elsewhere in OneLake. 
Figure: Select the Lakehouse that exposes the reference data.Figure: Choose the Delta table to use as the reference source.

3. Load only the columns the pipeline needs and preview the data. After selecting the required columns, open the data preview to confirm the schema and check a few rows. In this illustrative shipment, TRL-4471 carries fresh produce with a specified transport range of 2–8°C for a Tier 1 grocery customer. That makes a 9.2°C reading an excursion requiring prompt assessment.

Figure: Preview the reference-data schema and sample rows before joining.

4. Join it with the default stream. Connect the default stream and the reference node to a join operator. Map the key columns and choose a left outer join when you need to retain readings from devices missing in the reference table; choose an inner join when only matched events should continue. Use the SQL operator for more advanced logic.

Figure: Configure the join between live telemetry and reference data.

5. Test and publish. Preview the enriched output on the canvas, then publish and route it to Eventhouse, Lakehouse, Activator or any other supported destination. As shown in the diagram, you can incorporate multiple reference data sources by chaining Reference Data nodes with join operators.

Figure: Test, publish, and route the enriched stream to downstream destinations.
 

Going further: SQL for advanced logic 

As needs grow, you may want logic beyond a simple lookup. For example, you might calculate an "out of range" flag in the stream and tag each event with the regional hub that covers the trailer's route. 

Add a SQL operator to your Eventstream topology and connect both the reference data nodes and the default stream to the input connector of the SQL operator node as shown in the figure below. Open the SQL operator in edit mode and add the data processing logic. In this example , the query enriches each trailer temperature event with shipment and route-hub details, then writes the result to EnrichedTelemetry. It marks the temperature as EXCURSION when it falls outside the shipment’s allowed range; otherwise, it marks it OK. 

SELECT t.deviceId, t.temperatureC, t.eventTime, a.trailerId, a.cargoType, a.customerName, a.serviceTier, h.hubName, h.onCallContact, CASE WHEN t.temperatureC > a.maxTempC OR t.temperatureC < a.minTempC THEN 'EXCURSION' ELSE 'OK' END AS tempStatus INTO EnrichedTelemetry FROM TrailerTelemetry t LEFT OUTER JOIN TrailerAssets a ON t.deviceId = a.deviceId LEFT OUTER JOIN RouteHubs h ON a.routeId = h.routeId Figure: Reference Data join using SQL operator to add context from multiple tables.

Keeping context fresh

Reference data doesn't stay the same for long. Trailers get reassigned, customers change, and new sensors come online. Set a refresh interval on the reference data node to reload the reference dataset automatically and Eventstream uses the latest snapshot of the table for new lookups. 

The same alert, with context

 

With enrichment in place, the alert now reads: 

"Temperature Alert: Trailer TR-0918 (fresh produce, transport range 2–8°C) at 9.2°C. Customer: Northwind Foods (Tier 1). Hub: Memphis. On call: [contact]."
There is nothing additional to look up and nothing to guess. Within seconds of the reading leaving the trailer, the team knows what's at risk and who to contact.  

Outcome 

What changes 

Faster response 

Alerts arrive with full business context 

One join, many consumers 

The data is enriched once in the stream, and every destination gets the same record 

Lighter device telemetry 

Sensors keep sending small payloads, and metadata stays governed in OneLake 

Figure: The enriched alert provides the business context needed for rapid response.

Beyond cold chain 

The same pattern works anywhere raw events need business context: 

  • Manufacturing: add the asset, production line and maintenance schedule to machine data. 
  • Retail: add product catalog and store details to point-of-sale events. 
  • Aviation: add aircraft type, route and gate to operational events. 
  • Energy and utilities: link meter readings to the customer, rate plan and grid area. 
  • Financial services: tag transactions with account tier and risk profile in real time. 

Get started 

Learn more: Enrich Events with Reference Data in Fabric Eventstreams - Microsoft Fabric | Microsoft Learn

If you find this blog helpful, please give it a thumbs-up! Have ideas for what you'd like to see next? Drop us a comment or reach out to askeventstreams@microsoft.com — we'd love to hear what real-time scenarios you're building and what topics you'd like us to cover in future posts. 

To suggest product improvements or additional capabilities for your scenarios, submit an idea through Fabric Ideas.

fabric_blog:bca544cd94f7.title: OneLake: The file system for agent-first data engineering
fabric_blog:bca544cd94f7.excerpt:
Software engineers are increasingly using agents to build software, and data engineers are no different. We want OneLake to help enable data engineers to develop software in this new agent-first era.

Think about how you work in a terminal: you use it to run programs that read and write files. Both the programs and the data live in the file system. Now apply that model to data engineering: OneLake is the file system, Fabric engines are the programs, and the AI prompt is your terminal.

Over the last few weeks, we’ve released several new capabilities in OneLake that come together to create an experience where agent-first data engineers can thrive. This blog post provides a rundown of those features.

Managing OneLake

OneLake now offers a remotely hosted MCP server (preview), so agents can explore and manage your data without installing a local server. The local MCP option remains available if you prefer. We’ve also added tools to the Fabric Core MCP server for managing shortcuts and OneLake security.

In our previous post, we asked an agent to document an open mirrored database. It found the workspace, discovered the table schema, mapped the underlying files, and checked replication health—all from a single prompt.

That same scenario is now possible through the hosted OneLake MCP server. Once connected, ask:

“Document what’s in the House Price Open Mirror in my UK Property Data workspace.”

Figure: GitHub Copilot documents the House Price Open Mirror by using OneLake table and file tools.

The agent uses OneLake’s table and file tools to explore the database and build its response, working within your existing permissions. The experience is the same; there’s simply no local server to install or maintain.

The addition of the OneLake security tools extends what you can include in the documentation:

“Use the Fabric MCP server to document the OneLake security rules of the PricePaid table in the InlandRevenueHousePriceData mirror”

Figure: GitHub Copilot documents the OneLake security roles and permissions applied to the PricePaid table.

Querying OneLake

Agents need more than access to data—they need to know how best to query it. How do you turn a natural-language question into a query that works with data anywhere in OneLake? Continuing the house-price scenario, suppose you ask of the inland revenue database:

Question: “Using the InlandRevenue mirrored item from the TomDemo workspace, tell me how many houses were sold in Hampshire in 2020?”

Answer: “18,193 houses were sold in Hampshire in 2020, counting detached, semi-detached, and terraced houses. Including flats and maisonettes, the total was 21,452.”

How does the agent know how to answer this question just by asking OneLake? Endpoint discovery.

OneLake now provides an endpoint discovery API (Preview) that describes the Fabric Native engines available for each item and how to connect to them through skills, MCP servers, or engine-specific endpoints. The API also returns the OneLake Table APIs and File APIs so any agent can connect to the underlying data either directly or through tools like DuckDB.

When you include a simple instruction to use the discovery API and load the returned skill for the default engine, GitHub Copilot in VSCode turns a natural-language question into a query tailored to that engine.

Figure: GitHub Copilot in Visual Studio Code uses endpoint discovery to identify how to query the mirrored data.

To query data through OneLake, the data doesn’t have to live in OneLake. Shortcuts allow you to query data anywhere without making a copy. Shortcut transforms allow you to convert data files into tables without writing a single line of code to create or maintain the tables as the files change.

To continue the property price example, let’s combine the data from our mirrored database with some data in SharePoint. Mirrored databases are read-only, so here we’ll create a new Lakehouse to bring together our data and run a query:

“Please follow these steps using the Fabric and OneLake MCP tools:

  1. Using my existing SharePoint connection, you’ll find a folder in my OneDrive https://onedrive.cloud.microsoft/xxx/Documents/SampleData/council-tax-2026-27 that contains CSV data, can you create a new Lakehouse in the TomDemo workspace with a shortcut to this CSV, please use a shortcut transform to turn this CSV into a table.
  2. Create another shortcut to the Inland Revenue PricePaid table.
  3. Answer this question: What is the most expensive tax Band D, where is it, and how many homes were sold each year since 2000 in those postcodes?”

Answer: “Dorset has the highest 2026–27 Band D charge in the dataset: £2,765.02 annually, shared across 13,275 postcodes.”

Below is the Lakehouse that was built containing a delta table of our CSV data and the result of the query:

Figure: Lakehouse containing shortcuts to the council tax data and the Inland Revenue PricePaid table.Figure: GitHub Copilot returns annual home sales for the postcodes with the highest Band D council tax charge.

Because this is a Lakehouse, it exposes a Spark endpoint, which allows us to run an analysis to check if there is any correlation between the median house price of an area and its council tax band. GitHub Copilot picks the Spark CLI skill returned by the discovery API to perform this analysis:

Question: “now use the spark endpoint to run a spark job to see if median house price is correlated to the council tax band of the area - e.g., do higher tax bands have more expensive houses. Start with a Pearson correlation.”

Answer: “The Spark job found a negative Pearson correlation: r = −0.562. Councils with higher Band D charges tended to have lower, not higher, median house sale prices.”

Figure: GitHub Copilot uses the Spark CLI skill to run a Pearson correlation analysis in the Lakehouse.Figure: The analysis shows a negative correlation between Band D council tax charges and median house sale prices.

Now, all that’s left to do is check the results!

Discovery API example

The following API call and response enabled the agent to follow these steps, without hard coding any knowledge of what Fabric item type provides which query engines. The following response is an adapted example rather than a verbatim capture.

From one prompt to your data

Combine catalog search in the Fabric Core MCP server with endpoint discovery and the returned skills, and an agent can find the data, connect to the right engine, and answer your question, all from a single prompt.

What skills will you build to bring these capabilities together, and what would you like us to add to Fabric? Try these tools with your own data and share what works and what’s missing. Your feedback will help shape what we build next.

fabric_blog:6eafeb6028b4.title: Modernize data integration strategy with Microsoft Fabric when using Snowflake and Databricks
fabric_blog:6eafeb6028b4.excerpt:
Challenges solved by Microsoft Fabric

Microsoft Fabric is an end-to-end analytics platform that brings together data integration, data engineering, warehousing, real-time analytics, business intelligence, and AI-related experiences. It has grown tremendously within the community because it is solving a key problem: lowering the integration tax across data and analytics systems. To understand the integration tax, consider a mid-sized or large organization that wants to perform analytics and data processing. It may use several source systems, an analytics platform such as a warehouse or lakehouse, and yet another platform or vendor for orchestration. To generate insights, the organization must integrate these different systems (hence the term integration tax).

Fabric brings together a broad set of analytics capabilities within one platform, which can reduce the number of separate integrations an organization needs to design and operate. You can bring data into Fabric, store it in a warehouse or lakehouse, query and analyze it with Spark or T-SQL, visualize insights with Power BI, and support real-time scenarios with Real-Time Intelligence. Fabric also interoperates with platforms such as Snowflake and Databricks, helping organizations unify data and analytics across technologies while minimizing data movement and duplication.

The following diagram shows how these experiences come together as part of the Microsoft Fabric platform.

Figure: Microsoft Fabric brings data, analytics, AI, OneLake, and governance capabilities together on a unified platform.

OneLake serves as Fabric's unified logical data layer. Fabric-managed data resides in OneLake, while shortcuts and some mirroring scenarios can reference data that remains outside OneLake. If one team owns the data and another team in the organization needs access, the second team does not need to duplicate it. Instead, it can create a Fabric shortcut and work with the same copy of the data.

Beyond storage, OneLake also enables data-sharing and governance patterns across domains and workspaces. Organizations can expose data through shortcuts while maintaining ownership within the producing team, enabling data mesh architecture without duplicating datasets.

Integration options

We have discussed shortcuts briefly. Now let's look at how they work and at the other options available for making data accessible in Fabric:

  • Shortcuts: Fabric lets you create a pointer to data in its existing location and access it without moving it. A shortcut is similar to a symbolic link or a Windows shortcut: the data source can differ from the location where users access it. For example, data can remain in Amazon S3 while a Fabric shortcut provides access to the required data. To users, the data appears to reside in Fabric even though it is retrieved from S3. Shortcut transformations also support selected transformations on shortcut data.
  • Mirroring: For supported data sources, mirroring provides you with a low latency option to bring your data into Fabric. Depending on the source system, mirroring either continuously replicates data into OneLake or exposes the source through metadata mirroring and shortcuts. This approach reduces the need to manage pipelines or infrastructure and can offload analytical workloads from the source system. For example, if source data resides in an on-premises SQL Server database, you can create a SQL Server mirror in Fabric and analyze the latest available data there.
  • Open Mirroring: This is an extension of mirroring for any data sources that are specific to your organization. Open Mirroring enables applications or partners to write changes directly into an open mirroring landing zone, after which Fabric converts and manages the data as Delta tables.
  • Pipelines: are an option when a solution requires explicit data movement, multi-step orchestration, complex transformations, or integration across multiple sources.

User layer: AI Foundry and Copilot Studio with data agents

Making enterprise data accessible in Fabric is only the first step. Once that data is available through a governed integration pattern, organizations can build AI experiences that allow users and applications to interact with it using natural language.

Microsoft Fabric Data Agents allow users to interact with governed data using natural language and can generate and execute queries across supported Fabric experiences. Data Agents make it possible to gain insights directly from data without building an agent from scratch.

After creating a Data Agent, you can publish it to applications or other consumer experiences. As shown in the AI Agent Decision Tree, several consumer-layer options are available. This article focuses on two: Copilot Studio and Microsoft AI Foundry.

Copilot Studio

Copilot Studio is a low-code platform for building agents that combine generative AI with enterprise data and system actions. It is a practical option for employee or customer self-service, support automation, conversational access to Fabric data, and workflows where an agent needs to retrieve information or invoke an existing business process.

After publishing a Fabric Data Agent, you can connect it to Copilot Studio to build a custom agent that also uses other data sources. You can then publish the agent to Microsoft 365 experiences such as Teams. This option works well for common, out-of-the-box scenarios that a large language model can support without extensive customization.

Microsoft AI Foundry

Microsoft AI Foundry is where you would go when you need more control over how an AI application or agent is built and operated. It brings models, agents, tools, evaluation, and monitoring into one place, while still letting developers choose how much code and customization they want. In the context of Fabric, a Foundry agent can use a Fabric data agent as one of its tools, so it can work with governed enterprise data alongside other knowledge sources and business systems.

This option is well suited to use cases that require greater control over model behavior, orchestration, evaluation, and customization. Microsoft AI Foundry is typically best suited for professional developer scenarios.

Next steps

Microsoft Fabric provides multiple approaches for connecting existing data estates to analytics and AI workloads. Start by identifying whether your scenario requires data replication, virtualization, or explicit data movement, and then use the decision guide to choose the appropriate starting point.

simon_willison:9b0f1b3870f8.title: Qwen 3.8 27B on my laptop can interpret model weights, too
simon_willison:9b0f1b3870f8.excerpt:
Yesterday's hot paper was Sparks of Weight-Space Programming: LLMs can natively read & write neural network weights by Rikiya Takehi, Jayden Teoh, Alex Zhang, and Omar Khattab. The paper (OK, the authors classify is as a "blog post", but it's paper-shaped) found that frontier models, in particular GPT-6 Astra, can both interpret and modify the raw weights of a machine learning model - literally a text description of the model containing a bunch of floating point numbers. I've been playing with one of the examples from the paper and I'm delighted to share that Qwen 3.8 27B running on my laptop can do this as well!

Weight-Space Programming

Here's the highlight from their abstract, describing impressive capabilities for GPT-6 Astra and coining the term Weight-Space Programming for when LLMs analyze and modify model weights:

Just by looking at the raw weights, GPT-6 Astra can tell what a network was trained to do. And without any environment feedback, it has no trouble writing, from scratch, small game-playing networks that outplay networks trained with PPO for 100 million steps.

Likewise, asked to make Qwen3.5-0.8B better at math without gradients, Astra identifies an issue in its weights causing reasoning loops that Qwen’s own model card warns about, and fixes this by natively editing 0.016% of the weights. With the same sampling settings, this weight correction raises MATH-500 from 7.9% to 48.1% and generalizes out of the box to instruction following, raising IFEval by 3x.

All of this is possible without allowing Astra to write training loops. It uses its reasoning to figure out what each part of a neural network computes, or should compute, and changes the weights accordingly. We call this Weight-Space Programming.

The paper combines two topics that I think deserve to be treated separately. The first is what models can do with raw weights without running tools or executing code. The second explores how well models, once armed with code, can run operations to update and improve other models.

spaCy author Matthew Honnibal called the paper misleading for conflating the two, and Sean Goedecke deconstructed the Qwen3.5-0.8B update example as taking the same steps that a human ML researcher would use.

I'm going to focus on the no-tools question, which I think is the more interesting of the two.

The paper presents the first question as Can LLMs understand model behaviors from weights? They trained four neural networks to play simplified 10x10 grid versions of four classic computer games - Breakout, Pong, Pac-Man, and Freeway (I had to look that one up, it's an Atari 2600 game from 1981). Then they fed those weights (as floating point numbers) to an LLM along with the following question:

The weights below belong to one policy network that was trained with reinforcement learning to play a game on this grid. Which game was it trained on? Work from the weights. You have no tools: no code execution, no calculator, nothing to run. This is a single response.

The GitHub repository that accompanies the paper is RikiyaT/lm_understand-logs. The exp1_which_game folder contains the prompts they used, with weights for the four games:

  • breakout/prompt.txt
  • freeway/prompt.txt
  • pacman/prompt.txt
  • pong/prompt.txt

I checked and, aside from the weights, each prompt is identical to the others.

Trying it out with Qwen 3.8 27B and other models

The prompts on GitHub are self-contained. My LLM tool has a -f/--fragment option which can be passed the URL to a text file to use as a prompt, which means I can run any of the above like this:

llm -f https://raw.githubusercontent.com/RikiyaT/lm_understand-logs/refs/heads/main/exp1_which_game/runs/breakout/prompt.txt \
  -m openrouter/moonshotai/kimi-k3.1-pro

This example requires the llm-openrouter plugin installed, and runs the Breakout prompt against Kimi K3.1 Pro via OpenRouter. Here's what I got back from Kimi K3.1 Pro, which successfully guessed Breakout after 9m 41s and 19,493 reasoning tokens.

But how about Qwen 3.8 27B? That's still my favorite model to run on my own laptop - it's just 17GB (I use this version) and somehow feels close to the leading proprietary models of 2025.

I fired up LM Studio, ensured Qwen 3.8 27B was loaded with a long context window (the default 8192 context failed with errors), installed the llm-lmstudio plugin and ran this command:

LMSTUDIO_TIMEOUT=900 \
  llm -f https://raw.githubusercontent.com/RikiyaT/lm_understand-logs/refs/heads/main/exp1_which_game/runs/pacman/prompt.txt \
  -m lmstudio/qwen/qwen3.8-27b

(I had to bump the timeout up using an environment variable, see this issue.)

After 46m 12s and 43,506 reasoning tokens, Qwen on my laptop returned a response that ended like this (here's the reasoning trace):

Game: A simplified Pac-Man-style gridworld: an agent moves through a fixed 8x8 maze with central and corner wall blocks, moving objects/ghosts, and reward targets/pellets.

Description: The agent navigates a fixed maze-like 8x8 board, using current agent/moving-object/previous-frame cues to move through corridors, collect reward-target cells, and avoid moving objects or hazards.

Confidence: 72%

This is impressive. I tried it on two of the other games as well. It identified Pong (reasoning) in 1h 4m 54s:

Pong — specifically a Pong-like paddle/ball game where the agent controls a vertical paddle on the right side and must move up/down to intercept or return a moving ball/reward object.

Description:

The agent moves a right-side paddle vertically to hit or catch a moving ball-like reward target moving across the 8×8 field, while a left-side moving object/opponent and wall borders define the play; reward is obtained by successfully intercepting/returning/scoring the ball, and missing or failing to hit it is penalized.

Confidence:

75%

And Breakout (reasoning) in 52m 25s:

Game: Breakout, or an Arkanoid-like paddle/ball/brick game.

Description: The agent is a paddle on the bottom row and moves left/right to keep a ball in play; the ball moves around the upper grid, and bricks/reward targets in the top rows give reward when hit, while missing the ball/hitting the bottom wall ends the episode or gives penalty.

Confidence: 88%

Qwen failed at the Freeway prompt, which didn't surprise me considering that game is more obscure than the other three. Here's that transcript - Qwen thought it was "A simplified Pac-Man-like grid game: agent moves 4-directionally".

The reasoning traces are fun to skim, and almost incomprehensible. Here's a sample:

What about agent channel0? We see some large channel0 rows near row8 col7/8 and maybe bottom? Let's list channel0 large: line436 input435 (row8 col7 ch0) -2.107,1.169,0.513...; line441 input440 (row8 col8 ch0) -0.376,0.010,1.564,3.855...; line445 input444 (row8 col8 ch4) 0.142,0.491...; line382? input381 ch0? Wait line382 input381: 381//5=76 (row7 col6), ch1? 381%5=1? 76 * 5=380, ch1. So not. Channel0 large maybe at row8 col7/8 only. Also top row? line44 input43 ch3, line49 ch3. Channel0 large maybe not many. Agent position could be near bottom-right? If the agent is typically at bottom-right?

That said though, I expect a sufficiently experienced human being armed with a notepad and a pencil could get there with enough effort.

It's a cool paper, but some of the wider commentary I've seen around it does not feel justified. I'm not ready to declare that the age of source code is over and our future involves incomprehensible machines editing their own model weights in incomprehensible ways.
